verses.1: Al-Mizan defines lahw as distraction from what matters, takāthur as rivalry in acquiring wealth and status, and al-maqābir as graves, figuratively death. It therefore reads the verses as condemning rivalry over worldly goods and adornment that distracts from God’s remembrance until death, leaving people heedless throughout life. It also reports narration-based accounts in which two Anṣār tribes boasted first of their living members and then their dead, while other reports place the rivalry in Mecca between Banū ʿAbd Manāf and Banū Sahm; these accounts connect the sūrah’s revelation with that contest.

verses.3: Al-Mizan says kallā rejects and rebukes distraction with unimportant things in place of what matters. ‘You will come to know’ is a threat: when cut off from worldly life, people will learn the consequences of their vain amusements.
verses.4: Al-Mizan says the repetition intensifies the prior rejection, rebuke, and warning. It records the view that the first knowing occurs at death and the second at the Resurrection.
verses.5: Al-Mizan says the repeated ‘Nay’ reinforces the refutation, and yaqīn is knowledge free of error. The omitted result of the conditional is that certain knowledge would occupy people away from boasting, rivalry, and acquisition. Some treat (102:6) as an independent oath, arguing that law makes its preceding conditional’s result impossible whereas seeing hell at the Resurrection is certain. Al-Mizan rejects the assumption that this sight must be physical: apparently hell may be seen before the Resurrection through the heart’s baṣīrah, an effect of the station of certainty illustrated by (6:75). Those absorbed in vanities cannot attain the certitude required for that inner vision.

verses.7: Al-Mizan glosses ʿayn al-yaqīn as ‘certitude itself’ and assigns this seeing of hell to the Day of Resurrection, while the first seeing in (102:6) is the pre-Resurrection vision of the heart. An editor’s note says that this contrast makes the present verse physical sight in the hereafter and supports translating the phrase as ‘the eye of certitude.’ The commentary records and rejects as implausible the alternatives that the two sightings occur before and after entering hell, that they mean knowledge then physical sight, or that repetition denotes the perpetuity of hell.
verses.8: Al-Mizan says the chapter’s threats appear addressed to all but truly concern those absorbed in vain rivalry; likewise, questioning about al-naʿīm concerns those so occupied with divine blessings that they forget their Lord. Al-naʿīm is unrestricted and includes every blessing. A thing is a niʿmah only when it accords with a person and benefits them through use that brings happiness; used otherwise, even an intrinsic blessing becomes misery. Humanity’s created end is nearness to God through servitude (51:56), His wilāyah over servants; He has provided inward and outward blessings for that journey. Obedience uses them in the way pleasing to God, whereas becoming caught by them is disobedience and missing the goal. Since humanity must return for accounting and recompense, and deeds are how blessings are used, being questioned about deeds is being asked whether those blessings were used gratefully or ungratefully (53:39-42).
